title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Return as Nvidia CEO if Asked
author: Kalley Huang
text:
Jensen Huang said on Tuesday that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board asked him to do so, in his first public statement since resigning last week.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as C.E.O.,” Mr. Huang said on Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as C.E.O.”

Mr. Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after he admitted he was unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times has reported that he had an affair with an employee at Nvidia , as well as a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence has determined is an asset for Chinese intelligence .

Mr. Huang has the backing of a number of allies in Silicon Valley and Wall Street. But Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating him, according to a person familiar with their thinking who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The board, which includes early investors and business partners who have been close to Mr. Huang for decades, said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee Nvidia’s national security policies, compliance with U.S. trade restrictions and risk management for global trade.

Mr. Huang’s allies started a campaign for his return to Nvidia over the weekend, saying his exit from the company would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race and blaming Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure. President Trump also said on Monday that he “would not mind” if Mr. Huang returned to his job and that he thought Mr. Huang had “learned a big lesson.”

title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats
author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
text:
St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.

Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.

Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.

In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.

“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.

Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

title: 'I've never had just a copy-paste season' – A pointed change for Aaron Gate as road evolution continues and track targets linger in distance
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
Last year when Aaron Gate stepped into the WorldTour with XDS-Astana there was no question about the team goal, and that was chasing points as the squad knuckled down to deliver a stunning turnaround in the final year of the three-year cycle to avoid relegation from the top tier.

Through that process Gate played his part by taking three ProTour stage wins, an overall victory, plus plenty of podiums and top-10 results while also supporting teammates to many more wins in 2025. It was also a schedule that, for the rider from New Zealand, was dominated by ProTour races, where it was easier to harvest points.

The freedom of escaping the urgent points push for the team, which still finished sixth in the rankings in 2026, meant they could channel those efforts in another direction.

"Once we secured that goal it sort of shifted back to 'OK, how do we win some big races on the world stage?', and 'how do we achieve that as a team'," Gate told at his season closing race of Le Tour de Langkawi in Malaysia. "And the nice thing is, we didn't lose any momentum."

They did, however, shift a number of pieces around the board and that could clearly be seen in Gate's schedule – with his tally of races suddenly flipping to two-thirds on the WorldTour, doubling top-level races. With that move, also came a change in how Gate was utilised, the impact of which was reflected in his results tally.

"For me personally, it's meant focusing more on supporting my teammates," said the track specialist turned WorldTour rider. "And it's been a great season with a good group of guys "

That support role was also clearly evident at his season-ending race, as the squad rallied around Matteo Malucelli at Le Tour de Langkawi for three stage victories. Last year it was a race where Gate clinched one of his season victories on the final stage, after Malucelli crashed out. This time it was all-in for the Italian sprinter who claimed the final victory for the team.

It meant that Gate walked away from 2026 without a UCI win on the road, a position he is unaccustomed to, but that doesn't mean he is looking back with any sense of disappointment at how the year has played out. In fact, he was quick to name a season highlight as starting the Tour de France for the first time as part of the lead-out support for Max Kanter, along with a number of other marquee race debuts.

"I've really enjoyed doing some bigger races this year," said Gate. "For example, the year before I went to Tour of Hainan and it was, of course, nice to win a stage and be on the GC podium there. But it was also nice this year to finally do Ronde van Vlaanderen and Paris-Roubaix, which were races that I couldn't do because of the calendar clashes the year before.

"So it's been a completely different season, but one that I've enjoyed just as much as any other, from going to some of the higher level races, but of course it is nice when opportunities are there. So it's not like I choose one or the other. I think for me, the enjoyment is in the balance of being able to do both."

One thing for certain is that Gate, who moved from being a track focussed rider to a more road centered athlete through his career, is far from stagnating, with no two seasons looking the same.

"It's kind of the beauty in cycling that you've got this huge variety, and it's something that I think is how I'm still enjoying it at my age," said the 35-year-old, who may have just recently joined his first WorldTour team but has spent well over a decade racing on the road internationally around his track commitments.

"I've never had just a copy-paste season like a lot of a lot of pros do … they can get 10 years down the road and still be doing the same season, more or less, their their whole career. It's nice that I get this variety."

Gate is signed with XDS-Astana through 2027 and trying to "get some longevity" out of his road career, where he hopes to keep showing his worth at the top level by both supporting his teammates as well as going for results himself. The Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, where he came second in 2024, is one race that he singled out as an event that suits, and where he would like to have "another crack".

Though, looking a little further into the future, the track goals haven't fallen off the radar completely either. The Team Pursuit bronze medallist at the 2012 Olympic Games also has four gold medals from the Commonwealth Games on the track, and was selected as the New Zealand Team flagbearer for the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.

"I've sort of been disappointed with fourth places in the last three Olympics, so it'd be nice to try and go back for another one in Los Angeles and try to win gold finally. It's the thing that's kind of eluded me, so it'd be nice to try again," said Gate. "That's the long-term goal, but for now I'm enjoying the opportunities that the road is presenting."

title: JJ Gabriel confirms Manchester United exit: ‘You gave me moments I will always treasure’
author: Press Association
text:
Teenager says ‘thank you for everything’ in video

JJ Gabriel has announced his departure from Manchester United by posting a farewell message to the club on social media.

The teenager, who has not played a competitive game for the first team, joined as a 10-year-old in 2020 but has been absent since he requested the cancellation of his registration in September before he turned 16, on 6 October.

It has been widely reported that he will join Real Madrid and while he made no mention of his intended destination, his goodbye video on Instagram appears to have taken him closer to a move to the Spanish giants.

Gabriel said in the video: “Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here I grew as a player and a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.

“You gave me moments I will always treasure. To every coach and every member of staff, to my teammates and everyone who supported me, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow.

“As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything, JJ.”

Gabriel had remained registered to United, who are understood to be ready to explore legal options against the youngster’s next club over a possible breach of regulations.

The 16-year-old is the son of former Republic of Ireland international, Joe O’Cearuill, and last season became the youngest winner of United’s Jimmy Murphy Award, for their young player of the year.

United had hoped to persuade the teenager to stay but it appears his hat-trick-scoring turn against Sabah on his Uefa Youth League debut, on 10 September, will be his final appearance for the club. Gabriel shone in that 5-0 victory although his representatives were disappointed he was not registered to play later that day in the Champions League fixture against the champions of Azerbaijan.

The teenager was due to appear in the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton the next week but had seemingly decided upon a new direction by that point. Gabriel would have become the club’s youngest player in a competitive match in that tie, having appeared off the bench for Michael Carrick’s side in an August friendly against Atlético Madrid.

title: Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message
text:
JJ Gabriel has confirmed his exit from Manchester United with a farewell video message in which he says the club will "will always be part of my story".

The 16-year-old forward, who has a verbal agreement to join Spanish giants Real Madrid, walked out on United in September.

He has subsequently been training on his own in Spain after relocating with his family.

The 50-second video montage, posted on social media, begins with Gabriel penning a letter to United, and includes some of his notable achievements, including coming on for his first-team debut during a pre-season friendly with Atletico Madrid in Stockholm in August, when he was just 15.

Gabriel then thanks United's coaches and staff, plus his team-mates as he "begins my next chapter".

He has not returned to United since scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game with Sabah in September.

Although United still hold the teenager's registration until the end of the season, it does not prevent him moving to a club in the European Union as he now has an EU passport through his mother, who is of Cypriot heritage.

Speaking to Spanish newspaper Marca earlier this month, he said his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

However, Gabriel has now broken his silence on his controversial decision to leave United, having won last season's Premier League Under-18 player of the year award, United's U18 player of the year award and been top scorer in a side that reached the FA Youth Cup final and Premier League U18 cup final.

"I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here, I grew as a player and a person, from scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy [Under-18] award . You gave me moments I will always treasure.

title: 2026 Rouleur Live Tech Gallery: Chinese Tech, Titanium Splendor, and Everything In Between
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
This Titanium Chiru Aerix caught my eye for similar reasons. Although in this case, the frame design is much more modern - especially given the quite lengthy headtube. (Photo: Ties Wijntjes/Velo)

This weekend, London was the host for the 2026 Rouleur Live . Although it is not the biggest show, there are plenty of beautiful bikes, bespoke frames, and even some new tech.

Rouleur Live has been on my wish list to attend for several years, and this year I finally made it out to the London-based show. I think there is no event in cycling quite like Rouleur Live. It combines live interviews with some of pro cycling’s greatest stars such as Mathieu van der Poel, Lotte Kopecky and Mads Pedersen, with a relatively small but tech-packed expo.

Besides that and maybe even more importantly, it is also known as the unofficial end-of-year celebration for the British bike industry. I am no Brit, but considering the vicinity of many different pubs around the show and the British knack for throwing a party, I felt quite compelled to finally attend the show this year.

Luckily, it did not disappoint on any of those aspects. In the industrial atmosphere of the Truman Brewery, many of cycling’s most renowned brands were present. With relatively little space, many brands made the most of what they had and brought out some of their fanciest, newest, and most fascinating tech.

Surprisingly, there were even some new products on display, which is not always a given at Rouleur considering the time of year. One brand representative managed to summarize what most exhibitors were showcasing pretty well: brands were celebrating this year’s achievements, or teasing next year’s novelties.

Besides, with an Italian pavilion and many British bespoke brands attending too, there was more than enough to feast the eyes on. Let’s dive into our tech gallery of one of the last bike shows of the season.

title: 13 Holiday Gifts for Gravel Cyclist for Every Type of Budget
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

Finding the right gear for the gravel cyclist in your life is notoriously difficult—mostly because their wish list never ends. Fortunately, we at Velo spend the entire year testing this equipment, so we know exactly what they actually need for a new year of adventures.

To help get the right gear into the right hands, I have put together a curated list of thirteen top-tier gravel gifts. This list covers a broad price range, features items that will impress even the rider who has it all, and includes a few deals to save you some cash along the way.

The Wolf Tooth DEL pedals are a piece of kit I cannot recommend enough—they are one of the few things I never ride gravel without. I use both the standard-issue alloy version and the premium Mark Zero titanium models. Both offer massive upside, making mountain bike shoes feel as efficient as road shoes on the flats, while remaining fully capable in mud, dirt, and ice.

Speaking of gravel staples, most of my rides with those pedals have been done in the Quoc Gran Tourer XC shoes. I have long been a fan of Quoc’s dedicated off-road line, and that hasn’t changed with this slightly stiffer XC version. While they might lack some of the hyper-stiffness of dedicated cross-country race shoes, the Gran Tourer is a 10/10 on the comfort scale and has proven to be incredibly durable. They are the perfect companion for everything from a three-hour adventure ride to a multi-day bikepacking trip.

Bikepacking is one of those things that people rarely do just once. If you are up for one trip, you’ll be up for the next one. A great rear rack only makes that more certain, and there are no rear racks quite like Tailfin. The only knock on Tailfin up until now has been the price. With the Journey Pannier Rack, the UK-based adventure brand finally has something at a lower price point. Now, you can get the same mix of functionality and craftsmanship that Tailfin has refined from working with the best ultra-riders in the world at a much-reduced price.

If you ride gravel, chances are you have been “darked on”—caught out too late without enough light to get you home. The Exposure Lights Sirius front light is built so this never happens again. This small light is brighter than it looks, easy to charge, and with the right mount, it stows safely out of the way to keep modern cockpits looking clean. Its industrial design adds a bit of bling to your setup, blending high-end functionality with a slick metallic aesthetic.

I never ride without a Dynaplug tool. For five years now, I have brought at least one of these small tools to fix flats on road, mountain, and gravel rides. It has saved me on a bikepacking trip through Ecuador and while road riding around my neighborhood. It doesn’t fix every flat, but dang, it will fix a lot of them. Most of that riding has been done with the exact same Dynaplug Racer Pro tool. So while the price seems high for one small tool, it is well worth it for any rider—especially gravel cyclists.

The Lezyne E-Drive pump has been an effective travel companion for me this year. It lets you inflate tires to precise pressures before riding, yet still fits in saddlebags big and small. It holds a charge well and, crucially, works with TPU tubes, which is key for long trips where you’re more likely to need a tube to save the day.

This might be a product of where I live, but on many gravel rides, the sun is the enemy. Long dirt roads often don’t offer a ton of shade, and the Velans 2 sunglasses from Sungod have been fantastic partners. The coverage is excellent, but they still breathe well at slower speeds. I have dropped them, shoved them in pockets, and sat on them, and they have survived without a single scratch to show for it.

Gravel clothing has a bunch of definitions. For some, it’s skinsuits and aero socks. For others, it’s baggy shorts and tech tees. Yet, for most, it’s just bibs and jerseys that work well for long rides. The Gobik CX Pro jersey hits the bullseye in this regard. It is a breathable, race-cut jersey that still fits exceptionally well. Best of all, the splash of color pops against everything from desert landscapes to dark forests, helping you stay visible to the few cars driving down odd dirt roads.

While I tend to skew toward the lycra side of the gravel clothing divide, I have loved this baggy piece of cycling kit for years. These versatile and breathable pants are great for everything from a long dirty day to travel, as the ventilation and zippered pockets are just as fantastic for the airplane as they are for the bike. I have two pairs, and I find myself gravitating toward them more and more as a comfortable alternative to leg warmers or tights on colder off-road adventures.

No matter what I do, I cannot quite kick drip lube as a part of my gravel cycling. Yes, hot melt tools like the Silca Chain Waxing System are highly effective, but they don’t fully stand on their own. Even a well-waxed chain occasionally needs a refresh on a trip. Out of all the options I have tried, I have found that Faast Chain Lube does the trick best. It lasts a long time, handles grit well, and feels very smooth. It even pairs perfectly with a Silca wax base if you prefer to use a hybrid system.…

title: Gran Premio NYC confirmed as fifth UCI men's race in US next year with sponsor search active to add women's event
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
The Gran Premio New York City (GP NYC) returns as a UCI one-day race in 2027, as organisers confirmed that a fourth edition is now on the international calendar for Sunday, May 16.

The 1.2-ranked men's race expects to attract a more robust field of North American and international teams as it is no longer an isolated UCI race as Battenkill's 1.2 event on May 22 in Cambridge, New York makes the pair of road races appealing as a doubleheader, separated geographically by less than 200 miles.

Professional teams at GP NYC will start approximately 10 minutes ahead of thousands of amateurs in the Gran Fondo New York (GFNY) on the George Washington Bridge, sharing an 85-mile (137km) road course along the Hudson River, through the towns and scenic countryside of Bergen County, New Jersey and Rockland County, New York.

It is the GFNY, which is the flagship stop of the mass-participation GFNY World Series with events in a dozen countries, that provides the infrastructure for the pro race to take place.

"The pro race only happens because of the Gran Fondo. We have 3,000 riders, so it's a busy day," GFNY CEO Uli Fluhme told .

"Without the structure of the Gran Fondo and the road closures in place for the thousands of riders, there would not be a pro race because the cost for the pro race alone would be a million dollars. It's feasible because you have thousands of riders paying for the race.

"So all those road closures, and what we tell local governments and police is basically the same thing. They don't mind the pro race, just more colorful jerseys, 10 minutes ahead of the amateurs."

Both GP NYC and Battenkill, as well as a few other US events, include amateur racing on the same courses on the same day, which the director for the upstate New York event likes as a great model for cycling.

"We're super happy to be back on the UCI calendar again, especially with the prestigious GFNY and Gran Premio just 6 days prior and a short drive north to Battenkill from New York City. It's a fantastic opportunity for bicycle racing in the Northeast to showcase the landscapes that both events represent: the magnificence of New York City and the rural terrain of the Battenkill Valley of upstate New York," Dieter Drake, president of Anthem Sports which operates Battenkill, told .

Having the GP NYC on the international calendar brings the number of UCI road events in the US for men in 2027 to five, with USPro Road Nationals in mid-June providing an additional opportunity for UCI points. For women, however, there are only three events with UCI points – Tour of the Gila, USPro Nationals and Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b AmeriGas. Both Battenkill and Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic provide prize purses and USA Cycling-sanctioned women's categories.

"Of course, we would love to have a women's pro race as well. We've put it out there to sponsors," Fluhme explained. He said the issue was to make the women's race safe as well as affordable.

"If we put women into this, we would be looking at having to start the women an hour ahead of the men, which means an hour extension of closures. We could start them right after the men or together; then we would need to leave an hour gap for the amateurs.

"So we estimate a cost of the women's pro race in addition at $100,000. We have not overcome that hurdle of the finance to get it done."

The official Team Presentation for the men's pro race will take place on the second day of the NYC Bike Expo, May 14-15, held at the GFNY Festival Village in Fort Lee, New Jersey, where the finish lines are based on Sunday. Confirmations of pro teams and more race weekend activities will be made in the coming weeks.

"This is a passion project. It just costs money at this point. But you know, I'm a lifetime cyclist, bike racer; I love pro cycling, so that's why we do this. And I believe in it. I believe in the concept of integrating the two, the Grand Fondo, together with the pro race because the Grand Fondo riders are the fans of the sport."

title: Wayne Rooney says he contemplated taking own life during playing career
author: Press Association
text:
Former England footballer opens up on mental health

‘It was probably the lowest point’ at Manchester United

Wayne Rooney has revealed there was a period in his Manchester United career where he contemplated taking his own life. The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, he was struggling with his mental health off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai.

He said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life. “I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with,” Rooney said. “Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well.

“I got to a place where you’re contemplating suicide. You just didn’t want to be around anyone. I didn’t want to see people in the streets. I didn’t want to go into shops. I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else [I] really struggled with it.”

Rooney, United’s record goalscorer, said the issues he faced occurred at the height of his career. “You don’t want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it,” he said. “Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man if you like for doing that.

“I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I’ve just had a young son, I’ve just been married. It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn’t. It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.”

Rooney, who is currently featuring on the ITV show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, credits his wife, Coleen , with helping him turn the tide. “Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it.”

title: 'Now time to get serious' – Tadej Pogačar wraps up off-season of travelling, running, and fellow pro's wedding, as 2027 preparations set to begin
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Tadej Pogačar has announced that it's "now time to get serious" as he calls an end to his off-season ahead of ramping up preparations for a racing return in 2027.

The Slovenian former world champion was forced to end his 2026 campaign prematurely after crashing out of the Vuelta a España. After recovering from his injuries, he has spent recent weeks travelling and enjoying time away from serious training and racing.

Pogačar's latest stop came in Ireland at the weekend, where he and his partner Urška Žigart attended sometime training partner Eddie Dunbar 's wedding in Killarney. He wasn't riding his road bike while in Ireland, but was spotted by several locals riding a mountain bike and going for a run in the woods.

"Now time to get serious. But before that, spent some nice moments around the world," Pogačar wrote in an Instagram post on Tuesday.

"Sometimes cycling gives you more than just wins. Thank you Eddie Dunbar and Niamh O'Keeffe for having us there on your special weekend (yes, Irish weddings are long)! It was sound."

In a change from two wheels, running seems to have been a theme of Pogačar's off-season, with a video as part of his post showing him on another run, by the coast.

Next up for Pogačar will be a return to serious training as he prepares for 2027, with a meetup with his UAE Team Emirates-XRG team for a training camp in south east Spain next month.

His early-season schedule isn't yet known, but he is set for a return to the UAE Tour in February, a race he's won on three occasions in the past. Last month, he offered a suggestion of his main goals for 2027 – the Tour de France , Vuelta a España, and the Road World Championships – but the full outline is set to be confirmed in mid-December at the training camp.

title: You Don’t Need Separate Bikepacking, Gravel, and Race Bikes. You Just Need the Shafer.
author: Alison Jaksen
text:
The Ari Bikes Shafer HP (Photo: Ari Bikes)

Let’s be honest: if you could have infinite bikes, you probably would. Unfortunately, most of us tend to be limited by our savings accounts, our garage space, and our significant other’s desire that we spend our money on literally anything else. That’s when an elegant all-arounder like the Ari Bikes Shafer comes in.

Part race bike, part gravel rig, part long-distance hauler, the all-carbon Shafer was designed to meld high-tech performance with backcountry durability. Better yet, it actually delivers. The first jaw-dropper is the weight. The Shafer’s featherlight carbon frame clocks in at just 2 pounds—nearly a half-pound lighter than previous generations—and yet has enough clearance for 700×58c / 29×2.25-inch tires. That means riders can line up at a race one day, then slap on some fat tires and disappear into the woods the next.

Weather-sealed downtube storage, tons of frame and fork mounts, and internal dynamo routing give bikepackers and ultra-distance riders the features they need to go further. Meanwhile, dropper-post and suspension fork compatibility (up to 60 mm) means you can tackle rough trails without having to swap out for a dedicated mountain bike. Five complete build options let you further dial in the components and suspension to your specific needs, and each bike is custom-built to the rider’s measurements. Fancy, huh?

At this point, your mind might be wandering back to that crucial first point on our list of bike-accumulation obstacles: expense. While everything about Shafer—from its sleek geometry to its high-fashion paint job—screams high-performance, the hang tag isn’t what you might expect from a custom build. In fact, the Shafer’s Sport model starts at just $2,549.

That accessible price point comes courtesy of Ari Bikes’s direct-to-consumer model. Every Ari is built, tuned, and test-ridden at the brand’s Utah headquarters. Cutting out the middlemen helps the brand dramatically slash overhead without sacrificing quality. Ari also backs its bikes with a lifetime frame warranty and a 30-day love-it-or-return-it guarantee.

Now let’s say you like the sound of all that, but there’s one more category you’re looking for in your all-arounder: pedal assist. Ari Bikes has an answer to that, too. The Shafer HP , a carbon-frame gravel e-bike, is an extension of the Shafer’s ride philosophy. It combines the same geometry and versatility with a lightweight, whisper-quiet electric motor that provides a natural-feeling assist on big climbs and longer rides. Whether you’re dialing in your fitness, committing to a long daily commute, or just trying to access different types of adventures, the Shafer HP gives you all the perks of the analog bike, but with way more precise control over your effort and speed.

With a 360 Watt-hour integrated battery and an optional 160 Watt-hour range extender, the Shafer HP can handle long days between charges. Meanwhile, its 700×58c tire clearance and suspension-fork and dropper compatibility give it all the rugged adventure performance of the original Shafer. Even better news: the basic model rings in at just $4,899—a steal given its outsized capability.

Yes, it would be fun to buy three or four more bikes this season. And if you’ve been looking for an excuse to dramatically expand your fleet, we’re sorry to say the Shafer isn’t going to help you build your case. But if you’re looking for a true quiver killer that’s going to help you save money, go further, and access just about every conceivable adventure on two wheels, well, you may have just met your new ride.

Ari Bikes is a Utah-based, direct-to-consumer brand selling bikes worldwide since 2005. Ari’s mission is to help people live better now by making exceptional bikes more accessible. Backed by a 4.9-star rating, Ari offers direct-to-rider pricing, custom setup, a lifetime and transferable warranty, and a love-it-or-return-it guarantee to help deliver on that mission.

title: Rapha Pro Team Shadow winter glove review: A good addition to the Shadow range but perhaps not the best value
author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
text:
58 grams per pair - Medium

Yes

Rapha resurrected its Shadow range of foul-weather and winter clothing last year, and has expanded it coming into this winter season.

Gloves were included in that expansion, and the brand has released the Pro Team Shadow Winter gloves, which sit alongside the Shadow gloves in the winter lineup.

The Pro Team Shadow gloves are, in the brand’s words, ‘engineered for hard training in cold and damp conditions’.

These are thinner gloves that are designed to offer good dexterity and protection from the elements. They are also, given their ‘Pro Team’ name, designed with more purposeful riding in mind, where hands will stay warmer when you are generating that little bit more heat, but of course, you can use them for anything.

My glove testing for winter is well underway for our best winter cycling gloves guide . Whilst there’s still some warmth left in the sun's rays in my part of the world (UK), I’ve sought out some freezing conditions to put them through their paces.

If you are shopping for a thinner pair of light/mid weight gloves this winter, this review should give you the inside track on some of Rapha's new Shadow products.

These are thinner gloves designed with more purposeful riding in mind; they are also well suited to slightly milder temperatures or riders who don't want or need too much of a bulky glove.

Rapha says it has used its ‘Shadow technology’ in the makeup, meaning the gloves feature its Shadow membrane and a DWR coating. The Shadow membrane is an in-house offering from Rapha.

Rapha lists a temperature range for these gloves of 0-7C / 32-45F. If you are going hard in the cold, that might be ok. It depends on the rider, but if you are looking at these gloves for general fall riding in cooler conditions, I would recommend wearing something warmer below about 5C / 41F.

There’s Japanese OCTA thermal insulation in parts of the inside, and what looks like the same grid-shaped fleece that features on the Pro Team Bibtights and Pro Team Shadow Winter Jacket; it’s good stuff, similar (if not the same as Polartec Power Grid) and has always kept me comfortable.

The gloves pull on, extending a few centimetres up the wrist; I've worn them over and under long-sleeve base layers, arm warmers, jacket sleeves. The length is good.

The index finger is touchscreen compatible, which is just as well as the gloves do need a fair pull to get on, especially if you are slightly damp. Rapha recommends sizing up if you are in between sizes.

Two fingers, the top of the thumb and the palm also have a series of grippy dots applied, and grip is good on brake hoods and bar tape.

The entire thumb is covered in a soft nose wipe material, which is great; it's nice to have in the cold, and I'm glad Rapha has included it.

There are also some pretty specific care instructions on the Rapha website. I assume to look after the PFAS-free DWR, Rapha says to wash in a laundry bag at 30 degrees Celsius, and to rinse twice after washing. You can also tumble dry to reactivate the DWR. If the waterproofing was amazing, I’d be more motivated, but I’m not sure I’m going to have motivation to rinse these things twice after every wash.

Branding is minimal, with a small Rapha wordmark on the outside of each wrist and the recognisable Rapha dashes on the little finger. Black and Laurel (a kind of light grey) colours are available.

I’ve worn these gloves across a wide range of autumn temperatures, from the low teens to five degrees above freezing and in the rain. One of the first things I learnt about them is that they are not a pair of gloves to choose for anything more than light rain.

Within 40 minutes, I had soaked hands wearing them in medium rain on a gravel ride, my first outing with them. They resisted water for a little while, but were quickly overcome and got pretty waterlogged. My lower overall off-road speed did lead to my hands getting uncomfortable. I felt the thumb-wipe panel was probably one of the main key weak points regarding water ingress.

For intermittent rain or light showers, you may be ok, especially if you are going hard, but they won’t stand up to much water, so bear this in mind.

In the cold, going hard, they perform very nicely. I wore them on my local chaingang in 5ºC, riding hard, and they kept my hands comfortable without getting sweaty, ditto for various sets of uphill intervals, which is pretty much what they say they will do on the tin.

A feature I really like is the nose wipe panel, which covers most of the thumb. It’s really soft, and just helps when you need to wipe your nose in the cold. It’s probably my favourite feature and has been well executed.

Putting the gloves on and off isn't the easiest; for instance, taking them off for uphill intervals and then putting them back on for steadier riding is ok, but that tighter cuff makes it a little trickier.

When you are just trying to crack on, little things like that can be annoying in the winter cold. Breathability is decent, though, so perhaps more riders will just leave them on, and generally I have too.

For general riding, in cooler conditions, they work well too; they are thin enough to provide very good control and dexterity, and do a decent job of keeping your hands warm and comfortable. As an autumn option, or a thinner glove for more intense riding, they do their job well.

These are fairly pricey gloves at $120 / £80 / €95. They are well executed, look good, and do their job well. However, the rain protection is minimal. Switching to a neoprene offering in rain may be the way to go, but that does mean buying another pair of gloves.

These are a competitor to the popular Castelli Perfetto RoS 2 glove; those gloves are designed for a similar purpose using Gore-Tex Lab's Windstopper and a soft internal fleece and retail for £85 / $95. Does that Castelli Gore-Tex Windstopper label just carry a little more weight?

Despite being a similar weight, there perhaps isn't quite the same amount of insulation as the Q36.5 Termico gloves , but those gloves don't have a nose wipe panel or touchscreen compatibility like these ones do.

These are a solid pair of gloves, seemingly good quality and well made, and they do their primary function very well, but you can achieve the same performance for less money.

A good pair of lightweight gloves from Rapha that do what they say on the tin. They provide good warmth, dexterity and wind-blocking properties in a neat package.

They look good and fit well, but aren't going to handle too much rain, so don't expect them to.

The Pro Team Shadow gloves will carry you through Autumn and Spring and down to close to freezing if you are riding hard and generating heat and don't want the bulk of a bigger glove.

Testing scorecard and notes A good design that does what it says on the tin. Some protection in the wet, but not very much. Nice subtle styling.

Not great, wet hands within 60 minutes in the rain. Although these gloves aren't designed to deal with lots of rain.

Good across a wide range of temperatures. These aren't heavy winter gloves, but offer enough warmth when riding harder in some quite cold conditions.

Comfortable with a great thumb nose wipe panel. Id maybe just like the wrist to be a touch stretchier.

A little on the pricey side, par for the couse for a Rapha Pro Team product. Good gloves, but you can achieve the same for less without doubt.

title: The U.S. Has a New UCI Gravel Race, and It Is a Stunner
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
In 2027, the US will have two new UCI gravel races, with Borderlands Gravel the latest to join the UCI’s selection of sanctioned gravel races. The race in Douglas, Arizona, runs along the far southeastern border of Arizona and Mexico, with a short stint in New Mexico along the way.

The 2026 edition took place on November 14th, and Velo was on-site to get a sense of the unique event that melds the area’s American and Mexican identities.

Next year, the race will use the same terrain, but with more at stake as it will be one of three UCI Gravel World Series stops in the United States. BWR Utah in Cedar City will be the other new addition to the UCI calendar, while Highlands Gravel returns for another year.

The course, which will be an early qualifier for the 2028 UCI Gravel World Championship, will be an 87-mile largely out-and-back course with 5,000 feet of climbing. Half of the route runs directly along sections of the border wall, with the race using the gravel service road that cuts through high desert vistas, washes, and creosote fields.

The second half of the out-and-back leaves the border behind and climbs its way up one of the “sky islands” of Arizona. The climbing is gradual at first, with 14 miles at 2%, before a 1.6-mile, 8% wall that crests just shy of 6,000 feet of altitude.

The elements will only add to the challenge of the day. This year, it was mud and wind that challenged the riders, with rare November rains soaking the course. In other years, heat and sand could play a factor.

The constant factor? The gravel road that cuts through the Coronado National Forest in the New Mexico portion of the out-and-back is some of the most spectacular gravel riding I have encountered this year.

From a racing perspective, Borderlands Gravel will continue to be one of the last gravel races of the year, and thus one of the first opportunities to qualify for the next UCI Gravel World Championship in AlUla, Saudi Arabia, giving riders nearly a year to prepare for the event.

title: Inspiring the next generation of mechanics
‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
author: Jessica Murray and Neha Gohil
text:
Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial

When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country.

The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence.

Then he came across Project Search, a nationwide year-long transition-to-work programme that helps young people with learning disabilities or autism move into permanent paid employment.

It changed his life and now Bowman is thriving in his work as a personal trainer at Pure Gym.

“Getting actual experience in workplaces, understanding how they function, what would be expected of me and how to interact with people, it was exactly what I needed,” he said. “And having a job coach who does half the jump with you.”

Alan Milburn’s report on how to get the UK’s Neets into work has recommended an overhaul of welfare support for young people , including moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to a new “youth allowance”.

In return, eligible 18-to-24-year-olds will be guaranteed a fully funded, six-month job if they have been claiming universal credit for 12 months. Milburn said this was about prioritising “their longer-term life chances” over “immediate shorter-term finances”.

Interns and staff at the Project Search course run by Phoenix College in Tower Hamlets welcomed the bold commitment to get more young people into work, but there were concerns about cutting support and the quality of job opportunities being offered.

Bowman said he disagreed with the proposal to cut benefits like the personal independence payment (Pip) for young people to help push them into work.

“I think alongside any workplace initiatives, Pip is still absolutely a must-have. I would argue it’s more important to have if you’re going to be engaging in a structured programme – for me, things like noise-cancelling headphones are essential,” he said.

“I need that funding more to enter the world of work than I did when I was sat at home playing video games.”

Staff said getting young people, especially those with extra needs, into a long-term sustainable job wasn’t as simple as filling a vacancy – many students need holistic support and extra help even once they’re in work.

“We’ve been noticing a lot more interns coming in with serious mental health conditions and that requires extra help,” said Renato Marques, principal of Phoenix College. “But here, even for our very high-needs students, everything is geared towards getting them into a workplace.

“They learn the job doing the job. A lot of courses say they are preparing students for work, but they are not taking them into work.”

Rather than studying at a traditional campus, their interns learn in classrooms hosted in partner businesses – including a global law firm, a large distribution company and Queen Mary University of London – and they rotate through daily 9am to 3pm work placements.

Over the past six years, 68% of students ended up in employment at the end of the course – four times higher than the national average rate of disabled young people who are Neet.

All graduates also have access to a follow-on service they can use for advice in the first few years of their career.

For students with higher levels of need, the college developed a pre-supported internship combining two days of workplace experience – supported by an on-hand job coach – with extra training in social skills and independent travel.

Osman Osman, assistant principal for Project Search, said Milburn’s plan would only work with better paid and resourced careers advisers in schools, and high-quality work experience and job offers.

“You see careers advisers managing schools with a thousand kids, and they’re expected to meet with every single one, and it’s a very, very hard job to actually get those young people work-ready,” he said. “We spend a long time building our young people’s confidence and skillset in the field they’re interested in.

“And any job offer has to be meaningful placements because inset days, taster sessions or a week’s work experience often lead to no actual outcomes for young people.”

Tawhid Ahmed, 21, said finding work or apprenticeships after finishing school had been overwhelming – he now works at Phoenix College after building confidence and social skills on the course.

“I have a learning disability, and it was hard because I’ve been rejected for so many jobs. The fact that I was able to find Project Search really was a blessing,” he said. “Now I do admin and I have really good colleagues who help and support me. I want to help students face challenges that I’ve faced as well.”

Businesses are also a key part of the puzzle – Milburn’s proposals included a raft of incentives to encourage employers to take on more young people, including tax breaks.

“Employers might scoff at the review because there’s a lot of expectations placed on them,” said Cigdem Yilmaz, supported employment lead on the course. “We need an army of people, maybe that’s people like us, to be working with employers until we can get more young people on to the ground. Otherwise it’s just going to be more of the same.”

Max, a 22-year-old with autism, is being supported by the Youth Environmental Service (Yes), which works with environmental organisations to create accessible and entry-level employment in the west of England.

The organisation, which targets young people from diverse backgrounds and those with disabilities, provides access to paid work as well as peer support networks, a transferable skills programme and one-to-one coaching.…

title: 'A special place in my heart' – Alexey Lutsenko returns home to XDS-Astana for a new role after racing retirement
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Recently-retired Alexey Lutsenko is making a return to his former team, XDS-Astana, for 2027, taking on a role as head coach after calling time on his 14-year professional racing career.

The 34-year-old spent all but the final two years of his career with the Kazakhstani team and retired in October as one of the most successful Kazakhstani riders of all time.

Along the way, he took 43 pro victories, including stages of the Tour de France and Vuelta a España as well as overall triumphs at the Tour of Oman (twice), the Arctic Race of Norway, the Tour of Turkey, and Giro d'Abruzzo.

Having spent the final two seasons of his career racing with NSN, Lutsenko is now heading back 'home' with XDS-Astana as part of the team's sports performance group.

"The Astana project has a special place in my heart. Almost my entire professional career took place here," Lutsenko said.

"This is where I achieved nearly all my major results and found a sporting family. That is why returning to the project, albeit in a new capacity, and continuing my career in sport beyond racing brings me nothing but positive emotions."

Lutsenko will work under returning General Manager Yana Seel as Alexandr Vinokourov reportedly takes a step back to focus on the sporting side of the team. He'll join another former pro, XDS-Astana Performance Engineer Alex Dowsett, among the sports performance group.

The team also counts some recognisable names among their directeur sportif group, including ex-pros Dmitry Fofonov, Peter Kennaugh, Dario Cataldo, and Alexandr Vinokourov Jr.

"I know that the transition from being a rider to becoming a team coach will not be easy, and that I will need time both to gain experience and to adapt to this new role. However, I believe in myself, my abilities and my knowledge, and I am confident that with hard work everything will work out," Lutsenko said.

"I know that I have a wealth of sporting experience behind me, which I would like to share both with the project’s young riders and with my former teammates and colleagues from the peloton. I hope I can make a valuable contribution to the team as we work towards achieving our shared goals in 2027."

On the road, XDS-Astana will welcome Anthony Turgis from TotalEnergies for 2027, while a pair of climbers – Lidl-Trek's Andrea Bagioli and Kern Pharma's Urko Berrade – are other notable additions.

Notable names heading out the door include Sergio Higuita to Caja Rural-Seguros RGA, Davide Ballerini to Pinarello-Q36.5, Harold Tejada and Clément Champoussin both to Netcompany Ineos.

title: Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
text:
Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast , external , detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

title: Time for Tour de France Hommes? Marlen Reusser Thinks So
author: ahood
text:
Marlen Reusser says it's time to call the men's race the Tour de France Hommes. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Marlen Reusser says it’s time for cycling to rethink how it brands races by gender.

Instead of having the Tour de France and the Tour de France Femmes , the Swiss star suggests adding “Hommes” to the men’s race, all in the name of fairness.

Speaking on the Domestique Hotseat podcast, the Movistar rider said her frustration peaked at October’s presentation of the 2027 routes in Paris, where Tour director Christian Prudhomme and Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse shared the stage.

“The Tour director comes on the stage and introduces the women’s Tour director, Marion Rousse, at his side. You feel like he’s ruling it all, that it’s his Tour, the men’s Tour, and we are guests there,” Reusser told Domestique . “Marion is also allowed to say something, to say hello, but we’re the guests.”

Reusser first raised the subject with Cycling Weekly in October, first saying she thinks “Hommes” should be part of the conversation.

Prudhomme has said the Tour de France is the traditional name for the men’s race, which dates to 1903.

Speaking to Cycling Weekly after last month’s route presentation, he said that “the Tour is the Tour, and we’re absolutely delighted that there’s another race.”

In French, “femmes” translates to women, and “hommes” is men.

Reusser was quick to credit organizers for the growth of the women’s race since its launch in its current form in 2022.

But she also wants that progress to extend to the language surrounding cycling’s races.

“But I wish that very soon it’s not the Tour, it’s the men’s Tour. And we are guests that can have a little Tour also, but it’s the Tour,” she said. “And you can check the dates, from this to this is the women’s, from this to this is the men’s.

“And it doesn’t matter, and it can be just as interesting, just as cool,” she said. “I don’t want to be a decoration of a male sport.”

The issue is becoming a talking point as more races and teams have both men’s and women’s events and squads.

Many of the major teams, like Lidl-Trek and Movistar, do not differentiate between the two genders.

Some races that have both men’s and women’s editions follow the pattern used by ASO. Other examples are the Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women or the Vuelta a España and La Vuelta Femenina.

Reusser told Domestique that tradition shouldn’t prevent change.

“Let’s say the UCI decided there is a rule that you cannot put ‘women’ or ‘femmes’ in the name of a race when you don’t have the same in the name of the men’s race. Then you could not say it’s tradition,” she said. “You would just have to change it, and I think it would go fast. It’s a matter of how much people really want to change stuff.”

Right now, there are no official UCI rules outlining how race organizers name their events.

Reusser — who cited her background in medicine — said words help establish the hierarchy.

“If we word things as standard men, we think standard men,” she said. “So if we want to have it different, we need to start wording things different.”

title: Wout van Aert seeking damages in bizarre case of Belgian municipal employee who illegally accessed personal information of 30 pro cyclists
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Wout van Aert is among several riders caught up in a data protection court case in Belgium after a municipal employee accessed the personal data of a host of riders.

The public prosecutor of the Belgian city of Mons has requested a sentence of 120 hours of community service for the defendant after he accessed the personal data of various people, including election officials and 30 bike riders, reports the news agency.

A host of leading racers have been caught up in the case, with the defendant having accessed the data of Van Aert, Remco Evenepoel , Mathieu van der Poel, Greg Van Avermaet, and others between January and September 2023.

"Initially, it was for electoral purposes. Then it became an unhealthy curiosity. I wanted to know where the cyclists lived," the defendant admitted, according to .

The investigation began after suspicious activity was discovered on the defendant's computer on the municipal system in La Louvière.

The municipality suspended his computer access before taking disciplinary action and later dismissing him.

As part of the case against the man, Van Aert and his wife, Sarah De Bie, joined as civil parties.

The pair are seeking a symbolic €400 in damages in the case, with their lawyer emphasising "the need to protect their privacy and that of their children", according to

Any damages would then be donated to charity.

text:
The inaugural edition of the Vuelta Ciclista a Canarias , set to be staged in January 2027, has been cancelled, the race's organisers announced on Monday.

The race, to be held on the Canary Islands 1,000km off the Spanish mainland, was set to run for four days between January 14-17 on the islands of Tenerife and Gran Canaria, with ambitions to expand to six days in the future.

However, the organisers have said that the race will be postponed "in order to ensure all the organisational, logistical, and safety conditions that an event of this scale requires". The debut edition will now take place in January 2028.

"Since receiving confirmation of the dates in the last week of September, we have been working intensively and at a demanding pace on all preparations: designing routes, creating professional race itineraries, and holding meetings with state security forces, the Government Delegation, and the municipal authorities of the start and finish locations in both Gran Canaria and Tenerife," read a statement from the organisers.

"Throughout this process, we have benefited from the trust and collaboration of public institutions, which have shown their support for the project. However, despite the significant work completed and the progress made, we believe that the current timeline does not yet provide all the necessary guarantees to ensure the optimal execution of a competition of this nature."

Showcasing the 'eternal spring'

The stage race was announced at the end of September, and in October, race organiser Noelia Pérez told that the motivation for staging the race was to offer an alternative to early-season racing in more remote destinations and to show that warm-weather riding is available in Europe year-round.

"Here we train in short sleeves and shorts 365 days of the year, and we wanted to show that. You have to see that to believe that," she said.

"Plus there's a lot of racing in Australia and the Middle East at that time of year, but this is for those who've stayed in Europe who say 'Ooh, let's go and find some warm weather in the Canary Islands'. Because if they're on the rollers training indoors on the mainland because of the cold, we've got what we call 'the eternal spring' here.

"Being the first race of the year also shows people what they can do in the Canary Islands as well."

However, riders will now have to wait another year to take on the first-ever edition of the Vuelta Ciclista Canarias, which was set to run as a 2.1 UCI-ranked race.

"Out of a sense of responsibility and commitment to the institutions, participants, teams, and fans, we have decided to reschedule the event for January 2028," the statement continued.

"Throughout 2027, we will continue working to finalise every detail, ensuring that the Vuelta Ciclista a Canarias becomes a resounding success for Gran Canaria, Tenerife, the Canary Islands as a whole, and – most importantly – for cycling and sport in general.

"This decision reflects our commitment to carrying out this project with the rigour, professionalism, and ambition that the Canary Islands deserve."

title: A More Precise Clock Is on Its Way
author: Penelope Colston
text:
The world has been undergoing change in everything from the climate to artificial intelligence — and soon time itself is expected to undergo a major transformation.

As early as 2030, the optical atomic clock is expected to become the primary reference for global timekeeping, redefining the second as an element of time and playing a greater role alongside the conventional atomic clocks now used to maintain Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, standards managed by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (generally known by its French abbreviation B.I.P.M.) in Sèvres, France.

These extraordinarily accurate clocks, scientists say, also eventually would assist and replace some of the atomic clocks now used in telecommunications, satellite navigation and other systems that depend on ultraprecise timing for synchronizing cellphone networks; time stamping financial transactions and tracking the movement of airplanes, cars and ships around the world.

In the countdown to the shift, optical atomic clocks are in production at many universities and research institutions as well as a handful of companies — including Rolex, which already has three that it uses to calibrate testing systems and to contribute to the computation of UTC. (According to Rolex’s website, one of the clocks was the first optical atomic clock to take part in the computation of UTC.)

“There are many different types of optical clock and many research groups and start-ups trying to develop or improve them and bring them to market,” Florian Schreck, the coordinator of the AQuRA optical atomic clock consortium, a collaborative project in Europe, said in an email.

While atomic clocks aren’t exactly sluggish — they break a second into about 9 billion parts, which scientists call ticks — their optical counterparts tick hundreds of trillions of times per second and are astoundingly accurate . Researchers say that if an optical atomic clock had started when the universe began, about 14 billion years ago, it would be off by just about one second today.

title: 'Our ambition is to build the fastest kit in the world' – Rapha returns to the WorldTour as racing kit supplier to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Rapha is making a return to the WorldTour peloton as the official performance partner to the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team.

The British company has been absent from the top-level peloton this season after its deal to supply the EF Education men's and women's teams expired at the end of the 2025 season.

Rapha and Red Bull have entered into a "multi-year agreement", with the company replacing Specialized as the team's kit manufacturer.

In announcing the deal, Rapha hailed Red Bull's willingness to disrupt the sports it enters, including cycling, "bringing an unsurpassed level of global engagement, scale and energy".

Meanwhile Ralph Denk, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe CEO, said that Rapha has proven "it can change the face of cycling".

Rapha, which was founded in 2004, entered the pro peloton with Team Sky between 2013 and 2016, and went on to outfit Canyon-SRAM from 2015 to 2022, and then EF from 2019 to 2025.

It is currently the supplier for USA Cycling across various discilines, with Brandon McNulty winning the road race world title in Rapha in September, but this marks the brand's return to a trade team partnership.

"Returning to the WorldTour is a hugely exciting moment in Rapha’s story. We are back in the pro peloton with one of the sport’s most ambitious teams, backing riders winning at the very highest level," said Christina Lindquist, Rapha's global marketing director.

'An engineering challenge'

The agreement was not billed as a simple supply relationship, but rather a partnership that will see new products be developed, with "a shared ambition to build the fastest race kit in the world".

The companies are approaching kit design "as an engineering challenge", as Rapha shares resources and expertise from its in-house team, while drawing on expertise from within the team, with Head of Engineering Dan Bigham namechecked as a key point of contact.

"Working with a WorldTour team of this calibre is an extraordinary privilege and a huge technical opportunity. We get to work with Dan Bigham as Head of Engineering, clothe the best in the world, riders like Remco [Evenepoel] and [Florian] Lipowitz, and put Rapha back where we believe we belong: at the pointy end," said Joel Natale, Rapha's chief product officer.

"Our ambition is to build the fastest kit in the world. That means treating it as an engineering problem and rethinking how cycling apparel is developed, so that every detail becomes an opportunity to improve performance.

"We are going to push the boundaries of what apparel can make possible for riders at the highest level, with innovations that will ultimately benefit every Rapha rider."

'Rapha was a true gamechanger'

Denk, meanwhile, believes the partnership can go beyond performance and help to increase cycling's ability to reach bigger audiences.

Rapha certainly shook up the cycling kit market when it came onto the scene in the 2000s and went on to produce some of the most striking kits in the pro peloton with EF and Canyon-SRAM, though the company has more recently faced challenging financial circumstances.

"As a team, we have a clear mission: to make cycling bigger and inspire new audiences to embrace our sport. Rapha is an important partner in bringing this vision to life," Denk said.

"The brand has proven in the past that it can change the face of cycling. Rapha was a true gamechanger, bringing lifestyle into the sport and reaching entirely new audiences. Now, we want to take the next step together and inspire even more people to fall in love with cycling.

"Rapha and Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe share a desire to do things differently and find new ways to move the sport forward," he added. "This partnership brings our performance ambitions to life while giving us a platform to transform how people see and experience the sport together on the world’s most visible proving ground."

We'll have to wait a little longer to get a glimpse of the team's new kits for 2027, with the new season's collection set to be unveiled in December.

title: Pochettino says he would tell Guardiola to take USA job
text:
Mauricio Pochettino says he would tell Pep Guardiola to take the United States job if the former Manchester City manager was offered it.

Pochettino, 54, is leaving his role as the US men's team head coach to become Manchester United 's new manager from 18 November, after signing a two-and-a-half-year contract until June 2029.

He takes charge of his final game with the US on Tuesday when they face Haiti in the second leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals in Cincinnati, Ohio.

Guardiola, 55, is taking a one-year sabbatical after stepping down as City boss in May.

Reports have suggested Guardiola could be a contender to succeed Pochettino in the US, although there has been no formal contact between the Spaniard and the United States Soccer Federation.

Pochettino told reporters on Monday his advice to Guardiola would be to take the role, "because it's a perfect moment to arrive at the federation."

Tearful Pochettino on 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Man Utd

The Argentine added: "Everything is on the right path, in the right direction.

"Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people - the players can fit his style."

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is replacing Michael Carrick at United. Carrick was sacked as head coach last week with the club in the relegation zone in 18th place.

His long-time assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez and athletic coach, 31-year-old son Sebastiano Pochettino, arrived in England following the US's 6-0 first-leg victory over Haiti in Miami last weekend.

Pochettino's first test back in the Premier League is an away trip to Anfield to face fourth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.

"They are in advance, they are preparing all there, because Wednesday when we will arrive, it is going to be non-stop," he said.

"For me, it's not difficult, I think we are well prepared to switch quick."
