title: Alonso, Loeb join Aston Martin for 2027 Dakar Rally
Alonso to drive in Dakar Rally for Aston Martin
text:
Two-time Formula 1 world champion Fernando Alonso will lead Aston Martin's attempt to win the Dakar Rally in January 2027.

The 45-year-old Spaniard, who drives for the British team in Formula 1, previously contested the prestigious rally raid event in 2020 for Toyota.

Aston Martin have struggled in the first year of F1's new regulations in the Adrian Newey-designed AMR26 car.

Alonso sits 17th in the drivers' championship, team-mate Lance Stroll 22nd, and the team 10th in the constructors', only ahead of last-placed Cadillac.

Alonso, who recently signed a new Aston Martin deal and is widely regarded as one of the biggest talents in motorsport history, is joined in the Dreadnought by co-driver Marc Coma.

Coma is a five-time winner of the Dakar on a motorbike and was also Alonso’s co-driver in 2020.

The two other cars will be driven by nine-time world rally champion Sebastien Loeb of France and current world rally raid champion Lucas Moraes of Brazil.

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula 1 with Aston Martin, I thought carefully about Dakar," said Alonso. "In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely.

"I have enormous respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it. Having Marc alongside me again is very important, and with Aston Martin, Prodrive, Sebastien and Lucas we have an exceptional team."

It will be Aston's first involvement in the famously gruelling and dangerous race and they will go up against more established Dakar teams such as Toyota and KTM.

Aston's Dakar machines will be prepared by Prodrive - who had considerable success in rallying with Subaru in the 1990s and 2000s.

Despite challenges on the tarmac in F1, Aston have enjoyed much-improved performances in the World Endurance Championship this year, including at the season finale at Monza last month through the 007 Valkyrie car driven by Tom Gamble and Harry Tincknell.

Alonso could even drive the Valkyrie at the famous Le Mans 24 Hours in 2027 - F1 commitments permitting - where he won with Toyota in 2018 and 2019.

The 2027 Dakar Rally will begin in Portugal on 9 January and after 12 stages end in Morocco on 23 January.

Last month it was announced Dakar would be switched from Saudi Arabia following the unrest in the Middle East because of the Iran war.

The race, which also includes other classifications of cars, as well as lorries and motorbikes, was traditionally held between Paris and Dakar from the late 1970s, but the route has been adjusted over the years for promotional and safety reasons.

Alonso's previous Dakar brought a 13th-place finish. A couple of crashes caused by inexperience of the event delayed him, but a second-place finish on one stage showed his pace and potential.

"Formula 1 remains my priority," he said. "But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I'm looking forward to seeing what we can achieve."

title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
author: Donna Ferguson. Photographs by Urszula Sołtys for the Guardian
text:
Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset .

“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.

One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.

The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”

The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.”

He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees.

Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.”

Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.”

He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.”

Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators.

Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing.

“We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.”

He hopes seed producers will soon develop an “orchard mix” of wildflowers designed to attract the beneficial insects that apple growers need, and produce enough of it to bring prices down and make the practice even more widespread.

Many independent growers are also experimenting with new methods of water management, Jenner says. “Years ago, you’d kick the soil and say ‘oh that’s a bit dry, we’ll water it’. Now, we’re using neutron probes to measure the water deficit and we’re trying to get the trees to hunt for water.”

This involves letting the trees become water-stressed, he says: the top 65mm of soil in an orchard is left to dry out, which encourages deeper root growth and reduces the need for irrigation.

Back at Myrtle Farm, Thatchers is also working to improve soil health through regenerative farming. Before any trees are planted in new orchards, herbal leys – mixtures of grasses, legumes and deep-rooted herbs such as chicory – are sown and the land is grazed by sheep.

“Their little feet pound the ground, which improves the soil structure, and they eat the herbal ley and then recycle it very effectively back into the ground, which also improves the soil structure. So where we’ve had fields that have been continuous cereals or maize, we’ve found that within three years, the soil on all the metrics that are important for growing apples improves by at least 20%,” says Thatcher.…

title: Why Hamilton is key to Bearman's future - F1 Q&A
text:
The 2026 Formula 1 season closes with three races in consecutive weekends, the first of them a night race in Las Vegas.

With the drivers' and constructors' titles won by Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes respectively, there remains a close contest over who finishes second in the drivers' championship.

Before the race along the Vegas' Strip, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Is Ollie Bearman's career in danger of stalling by being at Haas and stuck in the Ferrari bottleneck? He obviously has the talent to be a world championship contender but being stuck at the back of the grid can't be doing his career any good. - Dave

Oliver Bearman has still not been confirmed as a Haas driver for 2027, even though both parties say that's what they want.

From Bearman's point of view, it's not hard to see why he might be asking a few questions about his future.

He is a member of the Ferrari driver academy and they show no sign of wanting him not to be, but at the same time they are not showing much sign of wanting to promote him to the senior team.

In that sense, Bearman's future hangs to a degree on Lewis Hamilton's.

Hamilton is talking about staying in F1 at least until 2030, which would mean a new contract at the end of next year, presumably with Ferrari.

But will Ferrari keep him? That is unknown, amid what has undoubtedly been some tension between him, team-mate Charles Leclerc and the team management this season.

If Hamilton stays, Bearman would be within his rights to ask how they see his future, and to ask for the chance to look for opportunities elsewhere.

How secure is James Vowles' position at Williams? He seems like a great guy, always very open and honest. But the fact remains that the team targeted this year for a big performance jump and they've actually gone backwards. Is Vowles running out of time? - James

Williams have had a bad season in 2026. There is no question about that.

For three years since Vowles became team principal in 2023, he had been talking about 2026 as the team's opportunity to take a significant step towards their ambitions of returning to the front.

Having finished fifth in 2025 - a result that even surprised the team - another step forward was expected this year under the new rules.

But that's not what happened. Instead, Williams have gone significantly backwards.

The car was late, too heavy and lacked downforce. Little relative progress has been made through the year and they lie ninth in the constructors' championship with three races to go and will almost certainly finish there.

All year, Vowles has been explaining that the new rules exposed pressure points in the Williams factory that he had not realised existed. Essentially, the factory systems were not able to cope with the demands being put on them.

He says they needed this experience to be able to fix them and move forwards to a better place.

A critic might question why Vowles had not realised they were there in the three years he had been leading the time up to that point.

Drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon have been unimpressed by what has happened this year.

But Vowles succeeded in getting both to stay on for at least one more season. Although whether that was because they retain belief in the team or because they did not have that many better options is a debatable point.

Asked what gave him the confidence to stay, Albon said: "This year I've been brought into a more deeper analysis of where it went wrong from last year to this year.

"So why were we late? Why was the car overweight? What were the reasons? Why did we miss the trick on even the philosophy of the car, for example?

"I'm satisfied with what those reasons are. As simple as that, really.

"At the same time, I also want to see these things materialise and I want to see these changes happen next year."

Albon admitted to there being a "deep frustration shared with the whole team that after all the efforts of prioritising this year's car, we haven't delivered a good job".

A new, lighter chassis was introduced at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. That will be carried over into next year so, as Albon puts it, "we start next year's car with a chassis that's not heavy, that's on the right foot, that we can then start focusing a lot more on not losing weight and a lot more time on aerodynamics and making the car go faster".

Through this season, Vowles has taken to publicly calling for a revision to the cost-cap rules, saying they bake in an advantage for the big teams, and wanting allowances for extra spending for others to catch up.

His critics say that those allowances are already there in one form, and that Vowles is using this as a distraction technique.

Whether his job is on the line if there is not a significant step forward for 2027 after all this is not clear. But the pressure is mounting, and he will certainly have a lot of explaining to do if there isn't.

With Max Verstappen established at Red Bull for the foreseeable future, what is Racing Bulls' real purpose: to discover Max MkII for Red Bull or simply provide a route to finding a reliable number two? Is it time Racing Bulls was allowed to operate as a genuinely independent, competitive team, rather than effectively functioning as Red Bull's driver development programme? - Michael

Racing Bulls' raison d'etre is the same as it has always been through all its name changes since Red Bull bought Minardi at the end of 2005.

That is to act as a training ground for drivers for the main Red Bull team.

It can be argued that the Red Bull young driver programme has not been especially successful.

In 20 years, the only top-line driver it has brought up through the junior categories all the way to being a success at Red Bull Racing was Daniel Ricciardo.

Sebastian Vettel was a BMW driver before Red Bull signed him, and Max Verstappen was plucked straight into F1 by Red Bull after winning a tug-of-war with Mercedes while he was in F3.…

title: Madison Huang, Jensen Huang’s Daughter, Became a Powerful Force at Nvidia
author: Kalley Huang, Tripp Mickle and Ryan Mac
text:
Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, Mr. Huang pulled out and tapped a longtime lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place.

But Nvidia hadn’t buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Ms. Huang. On a call ahead of the event, Ms. Huang berated other employees — including Mr. Puri — for being unprepared, said three people familiar with the meeting. Eventually, Mr. Puri interrupted and told Ms. Huang he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him.

Less than six months later, Mr. Puri left his role at Nvidia.

The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Ms. Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Mr. Huang resigned last week, she had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives.

That influence creates an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, who replaced Mr. Huang after his resignation last week. Ms. Kress must quickly determine how much power Ms. Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. She must also decide what to do about Mr. Huang’s other family members employed at the company: his son, Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez.

Mr. Huang resigned after revelations that he had had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer that U.S. intelligence concluded was working for Chinese intelligence .

The continued presence of Ms. Huang has raised concerns among senior executives that she has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father. Those concerns were heightened over the last few days as Mr. Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street started a campaign to reinstate him, and President Trump said he “ would not mind ” if Mr. Huang returned to his job.
